qs.q: What is the typical consequence of bilateral lower urinary tract obstruction caused by prostatic nodular hyperplasia?
qs.e: Obstruction raises intravesical pressure, which leads to detrusor muscle hypertrophy and can cause acquired bladder diverticula. Prostatic enlargement is a distal obstruction in men rather than a congenital anomaly like UPJ obstruction.
qs.s: Disorders of the lower urinary tract — revision: MCQs

qs.q: A 68-year-old man is evaluated for lower urinary tract symptoms, and an enlarged prostate is noted. Benign prostatic hyperplasia characteristically originates in which zone of the prostate gland?
qs.e: Benign prostatic hyperplasia typically arises in the inner or transitional zone of the prostate, forming well-circumscribed nodules. In contrast, prostate carcinoma most commonly originates in the outer or peripheral zone.
qs.s: Quick Guide: Male Reproductive System Pathology, Testis, Penis: MCQs

qs.q: A 40-year-old man is evaluated for lower urinary tract symptoms and pelvic pain. Extensive workup reveals no identifiable bacterial pathogen, and leukocytes are absent from his expressed prostatic secretions. What is the most likely category of his condition?
qs.e: Chronic nonbacterial prostatitis (CPPS) accounts for 90-95% of prostatitis cases and lacks an identifiable pathogen. Acute and chronic bacterial types are caused by common uropathogens.
qs.s: Quick Guide: Male Reproductive System Pathology, Testis, Penis: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old man undergoes evaluation for lower urinary tract symptoms, including hesitancy and a weak urinary stream. Urologic workup confirms Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH). Within which zone of the prostate does BPH characteristically arise?
qs.e: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia specifically arises in the transition zone of the prostate that surrounds the urethra, leading to urethral compression. In contrast, prostate carcinoma typically arises in the peripheral zone.
qs.s: Female & Male Genital Pathology: Ulcers, HPV, Endometriosis,: MCQs

qs.q: A 70-year-old man is evaluated for lower urinary tract symptoms due to benign prostatic hyperplasia. Microscopic examination of his resected prostate tissue reveals inspissated proteinaceous secretions within the glandular lumina. What are these characteristic structures called?
qs.e: Corpora amylacea are inspissated proteinaceous secretions found in glandular lumina during microscopic analysis of BPH. They are distinct from psammoma bodies seen in papillary thyroid or ovarian carcinomas.

qs.q: A 55-year-old man undergoes evaluation for lower urinary tract symptoms, and his medical therapy includes finasteride. What is the precise mechanism of action of this pharmacological agent?
o: Blockade of alpha-1 receptors to relax smooth muscle
Antagonism of androgen receptors on epithelial cells
Suppression of luteinizing hormone from the pituitary
qs.e: Finasteride is a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor that lowers intraprostatic dihydrotestosterone levels. Alpha-1 blockers like tamsulosin act by relaxing smooth muscle rather than inhibiting DHT synthesis.
qs.s: Penile & Testicular Pathologies: Hypospadias, Tumors, Torsion – Male: MCQs

qs.q: A 70-year-old man is treated for lower urinary tract symptoms caused by benign prostatic hyperplasia. Which pharmacological agent acts specifically by inhibiting the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone?
qs.e: Finasteride is a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor that blocks the conversion of testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone, which drives BPH. Tamsulosin (Flomax) relaxes smooth muscle via alpha-1 adrenergic blockade instead.
qs.s: Male Reproductive Pathology: Core Conditions: MCQs

qs.q: A 7-year-old boy with a history of chronic lower urinary tract obstruction undergoes cystoscopy, which reveals multiple outpouchings of the detrusor muscle between muscle bundles. What is the underlying etiology of these secondary bladder diverticula?
o: Abnormal dorsal fusion of the meatus
Incomplete closure of the embryonic urachus
qs.e: Secondary or acquired bladder diverticula are typically the result of bladder outlet obstruction (such as an enlarged prostate, scarred urethra, or posterior urethral valves) or bladder dysfunction from nerve injury. Primary diverticula are congenital and solitary.

es.q: List the typical clinical features of lower urinary tract infections (cystitis and urethritis) and common differential diagnoses.
es.m:
- **Irritative voiding symptoms:** Includes frequency of micturition, urgency, and dysuria.
- **Pain and spasm:** Suprapubic pain during and after voiding, and strangury (intense desire to pass more urine after micturition due to inflamed bladder wall spasm).
- **Urine characteristics:** Cloudy urine, unpleasant urine odour, and microscopic or visible haematuria.
- **Differential diagnoses (LUTI):** Urethritis due to sexually transmitted diseases (notably Chlamydia) and Reiter’s syndrome.
- **Physical findings:** May include a distended bladder, urethral discharge, or suprapubic/abdominal pain.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Lower urinary tract pathology covers diseases of the ureters, bladder and urethra, from infections to malignancy. Clinicians must link symptoms to anatomical sites, use targeted tests, and treat underlying causes while monitoring for complications.

sections.p: Lower urinary tract disease refers to any pathology affecting the ureters, bladder or urethra that alters urine flow or storage.
b: Includes cystitis, ureteral obstruction, bladder cancer, urethral stricture

sections.p: Staging follows organ‑specific systems: bladder cancer uses TNM, ureteral obstruction graded by degree of hydronephrosis, and urethral strictures staged by length and severity.

Infections dominate in low‑resource settings; bacterial cystitis, schistosomiasis, HIV‑related urethritis, and TB urethritis are common. Non‑infectious causes include stones, trauma, and congenital anomalies.

Symptoms vary with site: dysuria and frequency for cystitis, flank pain and oliguria for ureteral obstruction, hematuria and irritative voiding for bladder cancer, and painful voiding or obstruction for urethral stricture.
Tests are chosen to confirm site, cause and severity.

t.b: Positive nitrites suggest gram‑negative infection; leukocyte esterase indicates inflammation
Normal bladder wall <5mm; >5mm suggests inflammation or tumor
High sensitivity for stones and tumors

faq.q: What is the most common cause of cystitis in women?
faq.a: E. coli infection from the perineum

faq.q: Why is schistosomiasis a concern for bladder cancer?
faq.a: It causes chronic inflammation that predisposes to squamous cell carcinoma

faq.q: When is a CT scan preferred over ultrasound?
faq.a: When stones are suspected in the ureter or when detailed anatomy is needed
